rows.question: How green is my home?
rows.answer:
Your Green Home Score
The green home score before the measures was 44/100, class Poor. The parts that pull it down the most are energy use per square metre, energy efficiency rating and insulation. After the selected measures the score rises to 70/100, class Good. The modelled EPC rating improves from E to an indicative D, with the SAP score going up by 15 points.

What is holding the score back
Key issues are EPC energy efficiency (SAP 48 (EPC band E)), energy use per m2 (148.4 kWh/m2/yr), insulation (walls Poor, roof Very Poor) and renewable energy (no renewables recorded).

Things to know
Warnings: The savings for double glazing, a heat pump and a smart thermostat use typical published ranges, not measured UK data. Main assumptions: 77/23 split of heating and hot-water gas, boiler efficiency 85%, heat pump efficiency 2.8, 3.0% of gas used for cooking and other uses and mid retrofit impact estimates. Because a heat pump is selected, grid electricity rises while gas falls, and the EPC rating may drop due to higher electricity prices in the SAP calculation. Note: Electricity bought from the grid goes up with this plan, because a heat pump runs on electricity. Note: The starting energy use is a benchmark: the typical use of similar homes in the region, not this home's meter readings. Note: Combined insulation and controls savings may be overestimated: in national measured data, real combined savings were lower (by 5.6 to 13.8 percentage points).

rows.question: What should I improve first?
rows.answer:
Recommended improvements
The measures are applied in this order: cavity wall insulation, then double glazing, then a smart thermostat, then a heat pump, then solar panels. They are ordered this way because insulation and glazing come before the heat pump because they reduce the heat it has to supply; solar panels are applied last because they only reduce the electricity bought from the grid. The priority for an EPC assessor is solar panels, then cavity wall insulation, then a smart thermostat, then double glazing, then a heat pump.

Not suitable or needs checking
None of the selected measures are unsuitable. The infeasible measures are loft insulation and solid wall insulation, but they are not part of the plan.

What is holding the score back
Key issues are EPC energy efficiency (SAP 48 (EPC band E)), energy use per m2 (148.4 kWh/m2/yr), insulation (walls Poor, roof Very Poor) and renewable energy (no renewables recorded).

Things to know

Main assumptions: 77/23 split of heating and hot-water gas, boiler efficiency 85%, heat pump efficiency 2.8, 3.0% of gas used for cooking and other uses and mid retrofit impact estimates. Because a heat pump is selected, grid electricity rises while gas falls. Note: Electricity bought from the grid goes up with this plan, because a heat pump runs on electricity. Note: The starting energy use is a benchmark: the typical use of similar homes in the region, not this home's meter readings. Note: Combined insulation and controls savings may be overestimated: in national measured data, real combined savings were lower (by 5.6 to 13.8 percentage points). A heat pump cuts carbon, but it can lower the EPC (SAP) rating, because SAP uses electricity prices, which are above gas prices; the modelled EPC change and the property-value estimate include this effect.
